hero.subtitle: HTTP over QUIC — eliminating head-of-line blocking with UDP-based transport

steps.label: QUIC 1-RTT Data + HTTP/3 Request
steps.description: First HTTP request in just 1 round trip

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
HTTP/3 is the third major version of HTTP. It uses QUIC (RFC 9000) as its transport protocol instead of TCP, fundamentally changing how HTTP data moves across the network.

HTTP/3 addresses the last major performance bottleneck of HTTP/2: TCP-level head-of-line blocking. Since QUIC provides independent streams at the transport layer, a lost packet only affects the stream it belongs to.

sections.title: QUIC Transport
sections.content:
HTTP/3 relies entirely on QUIC for transport, which provides:

Stream Multiplexing
QUIC natively supports multiplexed streams, so HTTP/3 does not need to implement its own multiplexing layer. Each HTTP request/response uses an independent QUIC stream.
Built-in Encryption
QUIC integrates TLS 1.3, so every HTTP/3 connection is encrypted by default. There is no unencrypted mode.
Connection Migration
QUIC connections survive IP address changes (e.g., switching from Wi-Fi to cellular), since connections are identified by connection IDs rather than IP/port tuples.

sections.title: Connection Setup
sections.content:
HTTP/3 connection setup is significantly faster than HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 over TCP+TLS:

Protocol Stack
Round Trips to First Data
HTTP/1.1 over TCP + TLS 1.2
3 RTT (TCP + TLS + Request)
HTTP/2 over TCP + TLS 1.3
2 RTT (TCP + TLS/Request)
HTTP/3 over QUIC
1 RTT (QUIC handshake + Request)
HTTP/3 over QUIC (0-RTT)
0 RTT (resumed connection)

0-RTT data is vulnerable to replay attacks. Servers must ensure that 0-RTT requests are idempotent (e.g., GET requests) and implement replay protection for sensitive operations.

sections.title: HTTP Framing
sections.content:
HTTP/3 uses a simpler framing layer than HTTP/2, since QUIC handles stream management:

0x0DATA — Request/response body data
0x1HEADERS — Compressed header fields (QPACK)
0x3CANCEL_PUSH — Cancel a server push
0x4SETTINGS — Connection configuration
0x5PUSH_PROMISE — Server push announcement
0x7GOAWAY — Graceful connection shutdown

HTTP/3 uses QPACK instead of HPACK for header compression. QPACK is designed for QUIC's out-of-order delivery model, avoiding the head-of-line blocking that HPACK would cause on QUIC streams.

sections.title: Request/Response
sections.content:
HTTP/3 requests and responses use the same semantics as all other HTTP versions (RFC 9110). The differences are in how they are transported:

One Stream Per Request
Each request/response pair uses a single bidirectional QUIC stream. Streams are fully independent — there is no ordering between different requests.
No Head-of-Line Blocking
If a packet carrying data for Stream A is lost, only Stream A is blocked while awaiting retransmission. Streams B and C continue unimpeded.

sections.title: Server Push
sections.content:
HTTP/3 retains server push from HTTP/2, with modifications for the QUIC transport:

Push Streams
Server push responses are sent on unidirectional QUIC streams, prefixed with a push ID that correlates to a PUSH_PROMISE sent on the request stream.
Client Control
Clients can set MAX_PUSH_ID to 0 to disable server push entirely, or use CANCEL_PUSH to reject individual push promises before the data is sent.
